passages.happening:
When Hezekiah hears the Rabshakeh's words, he tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and goes into the house of the LORD (verse 1). He sends his officials and the leading priests, all in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz (verse 2). ‘Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them’ (verse 3). Perhaps the LORD will hear the words spoken ‘to defy the living God’ (verse 4). ‘Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives’ (verse 4).

Isaiah sends back the LORD's word: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard’ (verse 6). The LORD will put a spirit in the king of Assyria so that he hears a rumor and goes home, and there he will fall by the sword (verse 7).

The Rabshakeh finds his king fighting at Libnah (verse 8). Sennacherib hears that Tirhakah king of Cush is marching against him, and he sends Hezekiah a second warning: do not let your God deceive you. The gods of the nations his fathers destroyed did not rescue them. ‘Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 18 ended with the challenge hanging in the air: which god has ever rescued his land from Assyria? This chapter answers it. It is the high point of Hezekiah's reign and one of the great rescue stories of the Old Testament, set against the fall of Samaria two chapters earlier.

Sackcloth, a rough cloth of goat hair, and torn clothes were the ordinary signs of grief and repentance. Hezekiah's picture of children at the point of birth with no strength to deliver them was a proverbial image of complete helplessness at the decisive moment. Twice the Assyrians are said to defy the living God. The word, charaph, is the word used when Goliath defied the armies of the living God. The remnant, she'erit, those left over, is one of Isaiah's great themes.

The events belong to the campaign of 701 BC. Libnah was a town in the lowlands near Lachish. Tirhakah, Taharqa in Egyptian sources, was a king of the Cushite dynasty that ruled Egypt from Nubia. He became pharaoh around 690 BC, so many scholars think he is called king here in anticipation, as the prince who led the Egyptian force in 701. Others propose that the text combines two campaigns, a view that has not won wide acceptance. Sennacherib's annals report a battle with an Egyptian and Cushite army at Eltekeh and claim victory.
passages.later: David had asked, ‘Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?’ (1 Samuel 17:26). A psalm sings, ‘God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble’ (Psalm 46:1).
passages.asks: Hezekiah's first move was to go into the house of the LORD and send for a prophet. Ask where you go first when the threat is real. And ask whom you would ask to pray for you on a day of distress.

passages.t: A letter spread before the LORD
passages.happening:
Hezekiah receives the letter, reads it, goes up to the house of the LORD and spreads it out before the LORD (verse 14). He prays: ‘O LORD, God of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth’ (verse 15). ‘Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see’ (verse 16). The kings of Assyria have laid nations waste and thrown their gods into the fire, ‘for they were not gods, but only wood and stone’ (verse 18), made by human hands. ‘And now, O LORD our God, please save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God’ (verse 19).

Isaiah sends word that the LORD has heard his prayer (verse 20). Then comes a taunt song against Sennacherib. Zion, the virgin daughter, mocks him. Whom has he blasphemed? “Against the Holy One of Israel!” (verse 22). He boasted of his chariots on the mountains and his cedars cut down, but the LORD planned it long ago (verses 23-25). ‘I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came’ (verse 28).

A sign is given: two years of eating what grows by itself, and in the third year sowing and reaping (verse 29). ‘And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above’ (verse 30). The king of Assyria will not enter the city or shoot an arrow into it (verse 32). ‘I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David’ (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Hezekiah does what the people on the wall could not: he answers, not to the Assyrians but to the LORD. Spreading the letter before the LORD in the temple brings the threat into the presence of the true king. The cherubim were the winged figures over the ark in the inner room, which Israel understood as the footstool of God's invisible throne.

The prayer is a model of Old Testament prayer. It begins with who God is, creator and king over all the kingdoms; it states the situation honestly; and it asks for rescue for the sake of God's name among the nations. The LORD answers because Hezekiah prayed. The title living God, chay, sets the LORD against the burned gods of wood and stone. A living God hears, sees and acts, which is exactly what Hezekiah asks.

The oracle is poetry, a taunt song in which the despised city mocks the conqueror. Assyrian kings boasted in their inscriptions of crossing mountains with chariots, cutting cedars in Lebanon and digging wells in foreign lands, and Isaiah turns their own style of self-praise against them. Assyrian art shows prisoners led by ropes fixed to their faces. The hook in the nose turns the empire's own treatment of the conquered back on its king. Sennacherib's conquests were planned by the LORD long ago; the empire was a tool in his hand, and its pride was a failure to see who really ruled.
passages.later: Isaiah had promised a future king: ‘Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit’ (Isaiah 11:1). Paul quotes Isaiah's remnant promise: ‘only the remnant will be saved’ (Romans 9:27).
passages.asks: Hezekiah spread the threatening letter before the LORD and asked that the nations would know who God is. Ask what specific fear you could bring into God's presence in the same way. And ask how praying for God's name, not only your own relief, might change your prayers.

passages.happening: ‘And that very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (verse 35). Sennacherib breaks camp, goes home to Nineveh and stays there (verse 36). One day, as he worships in the temple of his god Nisroch, two of his sons kill him and escape to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon reigns (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
The chapter closes with brief narrative that fulfills the promises exactly: the rumor, the return home, the sword.

Sennacherib's annals say that Hezekiah was shut up in Jerusalem and paid tribute, but they never claim the city was taken, an unusual silence in Assyrian royal inscriptions. The Greek historian Herodotus kept an Egyptian story that Sennacherib's army had to retreat after mice overran its camp in the night, and some have connected it with this verse, though the link is uncertain. Babylonian records confirm that Sennacherib was killed by a son in a rebellion in 681 BC, about twenty years after this campaign, and that Esarhaddon took the throne. Kings folds those two decades into one verse. The god Nisroch has not been identified with certainty.
passages.later: At the threshing floor of Araunah, ‘the angel stretched out his hand to destroy Jerusalem’, and the LORD said, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” (2 Samuel 24:16).
passages.hard:
Did the angel of the LORD really strike down 185,000 Assyrians in one night, and how should a reader think about it?

Readers take verse 35 in several ways. Many accept it as a direct act of God, as the text plainly presents it. Others, who also accept that God acted, suggest that he did so through a sudden plague in the camp, noting that the angel of the LORD is linked with plague elsewhere. Some scholars question the size of the number, since the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a military unit, which would make the figure smaller. What is historically secure is that Sennacherib did not take Jerusalem, that his own records claim only tribute, and that he went home.

The moral question is real, since those who died were soldiers carrying out their king's orders. The text presents the event as judgment on an empire that had destroyed nation after nation and mocked God, and as the defense of a people who had no other help. It does not invite anyone to celebrate the dead, and its attention stays on the pride of the king who sent them. It gives no one a warrant to cheer the death of enemies, or to claim God's hand behind a war of their own.
passages.asks: Sennacherib thought his victories were his own, and died in the temple of his own god. Ask where you take credit for what God has given. And ask what it would mean to grieve even the losses of those who stood against you.
